plan.title: fix(hooks): pin-mismatch install recovery on a host that reports no run directory (Codex)

narratives.Description: After a pin bump the hook refuses every shell command until the project's packages are installed again. On a host that does not report where a command runs (Codex), the hook also refuses the install itself, and the refusal names no directory and no exact command, so nobody can follow it. This story keeps the admit as it is and rewrites the pin-mismatch-only refusal: a labelled project-root line, an instruction to use a terminal outside the blocked session at that directory, the plain install of the package manager whose lockfile is at that root, and a retry note.
narratives.Overview:
1. The pin-mismatch recovery admit does not change. The three exact commands, the simple-command grammar and the run-directory proof stay as they are. No install form that names its own directory (`--dir`, `--prefix`, `-C`) is admitted. A plain `pnpm install` stays refused inside the session.
2. Root line. When pin mismatch is the only fault, the refusal shows the project root that the hook resolved and passed to the install check, after the existing launching-checkout guard. It is a labelled line of its own, with control characters escaped, and it is not placed inside shell syntax. No second root resolver is added.
3. Where to run. The text says to open a terminal outside the blocked agent session at that directory.
4. Command by package manager only. The refusal uses `readLockfileRuntimeVersion` at that root for its `kind` and ignores the version it returns. Kind `pnpm` gives the command `pnpm install`. Kind `npm` gives the command `npm install`. Kind `absent` gives no exact command: the text says that no lockfile was found at that directory and tells the reader to run the project's own install from the directory that holds its lockfile. For `pnpm` and `npm` the text adds one sentence: the frozen form (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` or `npm ci`) can be used instead when the lockfile already records the pin.
5. After the install. The text says to retry the command once the installed runtime matches the pin, that this pin-mismatch check needs no session restart, and that normal checks still apply.
6. The overlay case keeps its own guidance and behaviour. The new text is used only when `pinMismatchOnly` is true.
7. Tests. A dispatcher test with host `codex` and a nested tool-input run directory equal to the project root asserts the allow decision for an exact admitted command. It is paired with refusals for an absent run directory, for conflicting run directories, for an overlay with matching versions, for the self-locating install forms, and for a plain `pnpm install`. The tests are named as dispatcher tests, not as live-host evidence.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a Codex session where pin mismatch is the only fault, when a shell command is sent with only the session directory, then the hook refuses.
- Given that refusal, then the message has a labelled line that holds the resolved project root and nothing else.
- Given that refusal, then the message says to use a terminal outside the blocked agent session at that directory.
- Given that refusal and a `pnpm-lock.yaml` path at the root, then the message names `pnpm install` as the command to run.
- Given that refusal and a `pnpm-lock.yaml` path at the root, then the message names no npm command.
- Given that refusal and only a `package-lock.json` path at the root, then the message names `npm install` as the command to run.
- Given that refusal and only a `package-lock.json` path at the root, then the message names no pnpm command.
- Given that refusal and both lockfile paths at the root, then the message names `pnpm install` as the command to run.
- Given that refusal and a lockfile at the root, then the message says that the frozen form can be used when the lockfile already records the pin.
- Given that refusal and no lockfile path at the root, then the message says that no lockfile was found there and names no exact install command.
- Given two lockfiles of the same kind that differ only in the runtime version they record, then the two refusal messages are the same.
- Given that refusal, then the message says to retry after the install, that this check needs no restart, and that normal checks still apply.
- Given a project root whose path contains a space, then the root line holds the whole path.
- Given a project root whose path contains a control character, then the root line shows it escaped.
- Given an overlay marker with matching versions, when a shell command is sent, then the refusal is the overlay refusal with the overlay guidance.
- Given the same Codex session, when the command is `pnpm --dir <project root> install --frozen-lockfile`, then the hook refuses.
- Given the same Codex session, when the command is `npm --prefix <project root> ci`, then the hook refuses.
- Given the same Codex session, when the command is `pnpm install`, then the hook refuses.
- Given a Codex payload whose tool input names a run directory equal to the project root, when the command is `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, then the decision is the recovery allow.
- Given a Codex payload whose tool input names two run directories that differ, when the command is `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, then the hook refuses.
- Given a host that reports the run directory, when pin mismatch is the only fault, then the admit behaves as today.
narratives.Constraint:
- Choosing the frozen or the plain install from the version the lockfile reader extracts (comment 6922252814 finding 1).
- A new lockfile consistency check in the hook path.
- Any install form that names its own directory, a compound `cd` form, or an extension of the simple-command grammar (first arc, comment 6908131375 findings 1 to 3).
- Using the session directory as the run directory.
- A second root resolver, or a root copied from a payload field for display.
- An exact command when no lockfile is found at the root.
- A promise that later commands are admitted after the install.
- A lockfile search above or below the project root.
narratives.UserStory: As an operator whose Codex session is blocked by a pin mismatch, I want the refusal to tell me the exact directory and the exact install command to run in my own terminal, so that I can clear the refusal without guessing.
narratives.ImplementationPlan:
1. packages/core/src/install-health/pin-mismatch-guidance.ts (new): `renderPinMismatchRecoveryGuidance(projectRoot, seams)` builds the text: a `Project root:` line with control characters escaped, the outside-terminal instruction, the command from `readLockfileRuntimeVersion(...).kind` (version ignored: pnpm -> `pnpm install`, npm -> `npm install`, absent -> no command and a no-lockfile note), the optional frozen-form sentence ("you can try"), and the retry / no-restart / normal-checks sentence.
2. packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts: when `cheap.pinMismatchOnly` is true, the refusal uses that text for the root the hook resolved (after the launching-checkout guard); otherwise it keeps `cheap.recoveryGuidance` (overlay unchanged). The admit is not changed.
3. packages/core/src/install-health/constants.ts: doc comment on `PIN_MISMATCH_PROJECT_PM_RECOVERY_GUIDANCE` says the hook renders the root-specific text.
4. Tests: core unit tests for the text; runtime dispatcher tests for the Codex refusals, the self-locating and plain install refusals, the nested-workdir allow, conflicting directories, overlay and a host that reports the run directory; update the two existing assertions that expect the old text (hook-dispatch.test.ts, hook-identity-failclosed.test.ts).
5. Release note as a changelog.d fragment.

## In plain English
After a version pin changes, the Directive hook refuses every shell command until the project's packages are installed again. It lets one thing through: the install command itself, and only when the hook can see that the command runs at the project root. Codex does not tell the hook where a command runs. So on Codex the hook refuses its own recovery, and the message it prints ("run the install in this project") cannot be followed from inside the session. The earlier design arc on #6337 tried two fixes. Treating the session directory as the run directory was refuted. Admitting an install command that names its own target directory was refuted for a relative directory such as `.`, which the hook and the command resolve differently. What is left is the same idea restricted to a full absolute path. The open question is whether that restricted form is really safe to admit with no proof of the run directory, and whether a fix that does not widen the admit at all would do.

## Pains
- P1 — On a host that reports no run directory (Codex), a pin mismatch traps the session: the hook refuses the install command that would end the mismatch.
- P2 — The refusal text names a recovery that the host cannot run as written.
- P3 — A fix must not admit a command that can install into, or act on, a directory other than the project root. The session directory is not proof of the run directory, and neither is a relative path.

## Out of this arc
- The `.gitattributes` and pack-render parts of #6337 (accepted there).
- Any change to which faults count as "pin mismatch only", to the overlay path, or to the global repair pair, which stays refused.
- Hosts other than those that report no run directory. Their admit is unchanged.

## Anchors at the dispatch SHA (claims, to be re-verified)
- `packages/core/src/install-health/recovery-admit.ts` (19-48): three exact token sequences are admitted (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `npm install`, `npm ci`); the simple-command grammar allows only `[A-Za-z0-9@/._=-]` tokens separated by spaces or tabs, so it has no colon, no backslash and no quote.
- Same file (68-73): the admit needs pin mismatch as the only fault, a shell tool, and `atProjectRoot`.
- `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts` `shellRunDirectories` (164-186): tool-input run-directory fields first; otherwise the outer `cwd`, except on Codex, where the result is empty.
- Same file `pinMismatchRecoveryAdmit` (194-225) and `rootsMatch` (131-141): every run directory must equal the project root after `realpathSync`, falling back to `resolve`, which resolves a relative path against the hook process.
- `packages/core/src/install-health/constants.ts` `PIN_MISMATCH_PROJECT_PM_RECOVERY_GUIDANCE`: the refusal text says to run `npm install` or `pnpm install` "in this project".
- `packages/core/src/hooks/tools.ts` (366-380): live Codex 0.162 PreToolUse input omits the `exec_command` `workdir`, and the outer `cwd` is the session.

## Measured outside this repository (parent, 2026-11-16, win32, npm 11.16.0, pnpm 11)
In a scratch pair of empty packages A and B, run from B: `npm --prefix C:/…/A install` and `npm --prefix C:/…/A ci` wrote and read `package-lock.json` in A only; `pnpm --dir C:/…/A install` wrote `pnpm-lock.yaml` and `node_modules` in A only. B was unchanged in all three runs. This is one machine and one version of each tool.

## Operator direction recorded for this arc
Prefer a design that removes steps over one that adds a gate. A new refusal needs a reason that no existing control covers. This path is a security boundary: the admitted form must be closed and must fail closed.

## In plain English

Codex cannot supply the directory proof required by the hook’s install exception, so the hook refuses its own recovery.

An absolute directory fixes the earlier relative-path defect, but it does not establish the proposed safety claim. The starting directory can still affect which program runs and what npm’s install scripts do. The design cannot bind on “nothing more than the existing install” as written.

A refusal that supplies an explicit external-terminal recovery can preserve the existing boundary and provide an operator escape. It does not provide autonomous recovery inside Codex.

### 1. blocks-the-design — An absolute npm prefix does not remove the starting directory from install behavior

Evidence at `72fe1658a04cef37d4dbea2bdad46ca087721853`:

- `packages/core/src/install-health/recovery-admit.ts:68-73` requires execution at the project root.
- `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts:203-210` supplies that proof.
- `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts:447-455` returns the recovery admission before setup or policy dispatch.

External evidence: the locally installed npm 11.16.0 source, `C:/Program Files/nodejs/node_modules/npm/node_modules/@npmcli/config/lib/set-envs.js:58`, assigns `INIT_CWD` from `process.cwd()`. npm documents both install lifecycle scripts and their access to the original invocation directory. [npm scripts documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/using-npm/scripts/)

Concrete counterexample: project A has a permitted `postinstall` script that writes a generated file beneath `process.env.INIT_CWD`. Today, the admitted install runs in A and writes there. Under the proposal, `npm --prefix /A install` launched from B runs A’s install script with B as `INIT_CWD`, so that script writes into B. No extra flag, relative target, compound command, or malicious dependency is required.

This does not claim installs are currently sandboxed. It identifies a new caller-controlled input that the existing directory check constrains.

**Disposition consequence:** target-directory equality cannot substitute for execution-context equivalence. The npm forms need a mechanism that preserves the relevant execution context, or the proposal needs an explicitly broader authorization claim. Empty-package measurements do not settle this counterexample.

### 2. blocks-the-design — The directory flag does not establish which executable runs

Evidence at the dispatch SHA:

- `packages/core/src/install-health/recovery-admit.ts:19-23,35-48` recognizes bare package-manager names and exact tokens.
- `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts:201-210` checks the shell tool, command text and execution directory; it does not resolve the package-manager executable.
- `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts:447-455` makes admission terminal for Directive checks.

For a Windows command shell that searches the current directory, B can contain an `npm.cmd` or `npm.exe`. Running `npm --prefix C:/A ci` from B can execute that program before any genuine npm processes the prefix. Microsoft documents current-directory precedence in command lookup. [Windows command-path documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/path)

The existing root-directory requirement limits this particular lookup exposure to A. Removing it admits lookup from arbitrary B. This counterexample is shell-dependent; it is not a claim about PowerShell’s default lookup behavior.

**Disposition consequence:** a host-wide exception based only on the directory token does not prove the stated boundary. A narrower design needs established executable-resolution behavior for its supported execution path. Otherwise, keeping the existing admission and improving terminal recovery avoids this expansion.

### 3. blocks-the-design — “Fully qualified absolute” is not a shell-safe path grammar

Evidence at the dispatch SHA:

- `packages/core/src/install-health/recovery-admit.ts:26-39` deliberately excludes backslashes, colons, quotes and shell expansion.
- `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts:131-140` compares filesystem paths through `realpathSync`, with lexical `resolve` as fallback.
- `packages/core/src/hooks/tools.ts:366-378` records Codex shell input without execution-directory proof.

If a Windows backslash form is admitted merely because it is absolute and matches the root, `npm --prefix C:\repo ci` passes a different argument through a Bash-style shell: unquoted backslashes escape subsequent characters. Filesystem comparison of the raw token does not prove the shell delivers that token unchanged.

**Disposition consequence:** the closed form must specify its accepted path representation, not merely its filesystem meaning. A conservative first form can retain the existing character restrictions and add only the drive colon needed for forward-slash Windows paths. Backslash and UNC forms, drive-relative paths, MSYS `/c/...` spellings, quoting and expansion need explicit support or refusal.

The token boundary also needs to retain exact arity and ordering: `--dir=<x>`, repeated flags, extra flags and reordered flags cannot become incidental parser aliases. Case changes, trailing separators, `..` and symlink aliases need deliberate treatment; `rootsMatch` alone is not proof of shell interpretation.

### 4. sharpens-framing — Terminal recovery relieves the operational trap, but does not make the agent’s command admissible

Evidence at the dispatch SHA:

- `packages/core/src/install-health/constants.ts:31-32` currently gives generic “in this project” guidance.

- The starting directory can decide which program named `npm` or `pnpm` runs. Under a Windows command shell, a file `npm.cmd` in the starting directory runs first.

## Summary

After a pin bump, the hook refuses every shell command except a named project install run at the project root (#6313). Codex does not tell the hook where a command runs, so on Codex the hook refuses its own recovery and the session stays trapped. This was split out of #6337 by the operator on 2026-11-16.

## What we saw

- The recovery admit needs proof that the command runs at the project root (`packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts`, `shellRunDirectories` and `pinMismatchRecoveryAdmit`).
- Live Codex 0.162 PreToolUse input omits the `exec_command` `workdir`, and the outer `cwd` is the session directory (`packages/core/src/hooks/tools.ts`). The hook therefore treats the run directory as unknown on Codex, and a test locks that refusal in (#4998).
- Grok is not affected in the same way: its outer `cwd` counts as the run directory.

## Context from the #6337 design arc

- Two critics refuted using the session directory in place of the missing run directory. The session directory does not prove where one command runs.
- The arc then proposed admitting the install command in a form that names its own target (`pnpm --dir <dir> install --frozen-lockfile`, `npm --prefix <dir> ci`). An audit found that a relative `<dir>` such as `.` matches the project root inside the hook and resolves elsewhere where the command runs (#6337 comment 6907435361).
- Candidate that has not been audited: admit that form only when `<dir>` is a fully qualified absolute path that equals the project root. The simple-command grammar would need a deliberate extension for a Windows drive colon, for that one token. The claim that the package managers honour the flag from any starting directory needs evidence from outside this repository.
- This is a hook admit on a path that fails closed on purpose. It needs its own design critique before it is built.

## Expected

The pin-mismatch recovery works on every supported host, or the refusal names a recovery the host can run, without treating the session directory as the run directory.

## Acceptance Criteria
